variables_mentioned: children (biological; in Norway legal children of at least one partner, including adopted children)
combined personal taxable earnings (Norway: earnings after taxes)

registers.name_in_paper: individual-level register data from Sweden (accessed through Statistics Sweden)
variables_mentioned: children (biological; in Norway legal children of at least one partner, including adopted children)
combined personal taxable earnings (Norway: earnings after taxes)

registers.name_in_paper: individual-level register data from Norway (accessed through Statistics Norway)
variables_mentioned: children (biological; in Norway legal children of at least one partner, including adopted children)
combined personal taxable earnings (Norway: earnings after taxes)

registers.name_in_paper: individual-level register data from Finland (accessed through Statistics Finland)
variables_mentioned: children (biological; in Norway legal children of at least one partner, including adopted children)
combined personal taxable earnings (Norway: earnings after taxes)

linkages: individuals linked through personal identification numbers to their civil status information, children, and other demographic and socioeconomic characteristics
same-sex couples identified from individuals' marital status and legal sex
spouses linked into couples; childbearing analysed at the couple level
harmonized across the four national register systems

sample.universe: all female same-sex couples who registered a partnership or married in Denmark 1989-2018, Norway 1993-2017, Sweden 1995-2016 and Finland 2002-2016, and all different-sex couples who married in the same periods
sample.unit_of_observation: couple (followed for five years from legal union formation)
selection_rules: both spouses resided in the country at the time of the legal union formation (couples with either spouse registered as living abroad excluded)
the union was the first of that union type for both spouses (previous same-sex union for same-sex couples, previous different-sex union for different-sex couples, excluded)
couples in which the youngest spouse was 45 years or older at the end of the year of the legal union formation excluded; for different-sex couples, the woman had to be under 45 in the marriage year
male same-sex couples excluded because so few have a child together that privacy concerns make reporting by socioeconomic status impossible
union-formation periods begin in the first year of registered partnerships in each country and end with the last year for which five years of childbearing follow-up exist
sample.period: union cohorts 1989-2018 (Denmark), 1995-2016 (Sweden), 1993-2017 (Norway), 2002-2016 (Finland); childbearing followed to the end of 2023 (Denmark), 2022 (Norway) and 2021 (Sweden and Finland)
sample.n_observations: 11,037 female same-sex couples and 1,754,567 different-sex couples

construction_notes: probability of having a child within five years of partnership registration or marriage estimated with the Kaplan-Meier estimator; couples at risk from the month of entering the legal union until the month of divorce, emigration, death of either partner, or the end of the five-year follow-up, whichever comes first
conversion of a registered partnership into a marriage during follow-up treated as a stable union
having a child = birth of the couple's first biological child after the legal union formation; if both women in a same-sex union gave birth within follow-up, the first birth is the outcome
in the Norwegian data, prior children and children born after the union are legal children of at least one partner, which also includes adopted children

prior children = any biological children born to either partner before the legal union formation (children born to the couple before legalizing the union cannot be separated from children of previous relationships)

couple education = highest ISCED level obtained by either spouse by the end of the year of union formation; low = ISCED 0-2 (including missing cases, i.e. education completed abroad, except in Sweden), medium = ISCED 3-4, high = ISCED 5-8 (the note to Figure 4 prints ISCED 5-6)

couple income = combined personal taxable earnings of spouses in the year of union formation, adjusted for inflation to 2015 levels; for Norway, combined personal earnings after taxes; income tertiles formed from the combined population of female couples and different-sex couples in each country; Table 1 also reports PPP-adjusted incomes (2015 index levels)

some yearly union cohorts are combined to ensure sufficient numbers: all Norwegian cohorts, and the education and income analyses in every country; the groupings differ by country and are indicated in the results figures

all analyses performed separately by country and by couple type; no regression table is reported in the main text, adjusted logistic-regression predicted probabilities are in the Online Appendix (Tables A1-A3)

claims.statement: In Denmark, among couples entering a legal union in the 1989 cohort, female same-sex couples were less likely than different-sex couples to include a spouse who was already a parent at union formation (20.0 vs. 45.4 percent).

treatment.label: Couple type: female same-sex couple (vs. different-sex couple)

register_source.value: Nordic population registers accessed through Statistics Denmark, Statistics Sweden, Statistics Norway and Statistics Finland; the paper names no register codes or register variable names; same-sex couples are identified from individuals' marital status and legal sex

definition.value: Female same-sex couples (two women who registered a partnership or married) compared with different-sex couples who married in the same country and period; same-sex couples are identified based on individuals' marital status and legal sex

timing.value: at legal union formation

outcome.label: Proportion of couples in which at least one spouse was a parent at the time of the legal union formation

register_source.value: Nordic population registers accessed through Statistics Denmark, Statistics Sweden, Statistics Norway and Statistics Finland; the paper names no register codes or register variable names

definition.value: Annual unconditional proportion of couples in which at least one spouse already had a child by the time of the legal union formation; prior children are defined as any biological children born to either partner before the legal union formation (children born to the couple before legalizing the union cannot be separated from children of previous relationships)

timing.value: at the time of legal union formation, by year of union formation

units.value: percent of couples in which at least one spouse was already a parent at legal union formation

magnitude.interpretation: female couples were less likely than different-sex couples to have a prior child by either spouse

estimand.target_population: female same-sex couples relative to different-sex couples forming a first legal union in Denmark in the 1989 cohort
estimand.time_horizon: measured at the time of the legal union formation

population.description: Female same-sex couples and different-sex couples who entered a first legal union (registered partnership or marriage) in Denmark in 1989–2018, both spouses resident in the country, younger spouse (woman in different-sex couples) under 45 at the end of the union-formation year
population.ages: younger spouse (woman in different-sex couples) under 45 years at the end of the year of legal union formation
population.selection: couples who formed a first legal union of that type with both spouses resident in the country; male same-sex couples excluded because too few have a child together to report by socioeconomic status; childbearing outside legal unions not observed

identification.source_of_variation: Comparison of female same-sex couples with different-sex couples who entered a legal union in the same country and the same union-cohort year; no exogenous variation is used

key_assumptions.assumption: The sample is conditioned on entry into a legal union: only couples who registered a partnership or married are observed, so childbearing by same-sex couples outside legal unions is not captured, and the authors state the group of couples studied becomes increasingly selected over time.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Strengths and limitations section; no test offered (the authors state selection cannot be estimated)

key_assumptions.assumption: The difference between female same-sex and different-sex couples is an unadjusted descriptive gap: the two couple types differ in the ages of the partners, in prior childbearing and in education, and these are not held constant in the reported estimate.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Online Appendix Table A1 gives predicted probabilities from logistic regression adjusted for the partners' ages, prior childbearing and educational levels; the authors report that these do not explain the convergence

threats_discussed: increasing selection into legal unions as childbearing became legally possible outside legal unions
compositional differences between female and different-sex couples in partner age, prior childbearing and education
small numbers of couples in the low-education groups in Norway and Sweden
sensitivity of the educational gradient to how education is coded
no information on sexual orientation, gender identity or parental desires
robustness_checks: predicted probabilities from logistic regression adjusted for partners' ages, prior childbearing and educational levels (Online Appendix Table A1)
education recoded into two categories, higher vs. less than higher education (Online Appendix Figure A5)
age-adjusted educational differences for female couples (Table A2) and different-sex couples (Table A3)
likelihood of a child after union formation separately for couples with and without a prior child (Online Appendix Figure A4)
PPP-adjusted incomes reported alongside nominal incomes (Table 1)
unresolved_confounders: selection into legal unions among same-sex couples, which the authors state is difficult to estimate without knowing the characteristics of unmarried same-sex couples
childbearing outside legal unions, which the data cannot capture
no direct information on individuals' subjective perceptions, such as sexual orientation, gender identity or parental desires
